rows.english: The marks and signs on the physical body of the Buddha are like an image drawn on a piece of paper: they are not the real thing--they exist in a deceptive manner, as things that occur when all of their causes have gathered together. They do not exist as something with a true nature. To indicate this fact, Lord Buddha says to Subhuti, "Insofar as the totally exquisite marks on a Buddha's body exist, as such they are deceptive. "Just what," you may ask, "is meant by the word deceptive?" The totally exquisite marks and signs on a Buddha's body are also not deceptive, and true, but only insofar as they do not exist truly. Thus you should see the One Thus Gone as having no marks, no marks to indicate his nature, at all. The section here helps to prevent us from falling into either one of the two extremes. The physical body of the Buddha and its various marks and signs do exist--albeit in a deceptive way, in a false or empty way--and this fact keeps us from the extreme of denying the existence of something which actually does exist. The text though also states that there exist no marks, and no marks that would indicate any nature, which also exist truly. This fact keeps us from the extreme of asserting the existence of something which actually does not exist. The former of these two [marks] is referring to the physical body of a Buddha. The latter is referring to the dharma body, and chiefly to the essence body. 38 The Asian Classics Institute Course VI: The Diamond-Cutter Sutra Re

rows.english: The marks and signs on the physical body of the Buddha are like an image drawn on a piece of paper: they are not the real thing--they exist in a deceptive manner, as things that occur when all of their causes have gathered together. They do not exist as something with a true nature. To indicate this fact, Lord Buddha says to Subhuti, "Insofar as the totally exquisite marks on a Buddha's body exist, as such they are deceptive. "Just what," you may ask, "is meant by the word deceptive?" The totally exquisite marks and signs on a Buddha's body are also not deceptive, and true, but only insofar as they do not exist truly. Thus you should see the One Thus Gone as having no marks, no marks to indicate his nature, at all. The section here helps to prevent us from falling into either one of the two extremes. The physical body of the Buddha and its various marks and signs do exist--albeit in a deceptive way, in a false or empty way--and this fact keeps us from the extreme of denying the existence of something which actually does exist. The text though also states that there exist no marks, and no marks that would indicate any nature, which also exist truly. This fact keeps us from the extreme of asserting the existence of something which actually does not exist. The former of these two [marks] is referring to the physical body of a Buddha. The latter is referring to the dharma body, and chiefly to the essence body. 9 On the Future of the Buddha's Teachings

rows.english: There are, moreover, the ten types of knowledge, which perceive the four truths and so on; these are: (1–2) the knowledge of things and also subsequent knowledge, as forms of spiritual antidotes; (3) the knowledge of the deceptive, so named from the sorts of objects it perceives; (4) the knowledge of others' minds, as this is needed to approach them; (5–6) the knowledge of the higher truth of suffering, and that of the cause of suffering, again named from the aspect of their objects; (7–8) the knowledge of the higher truth of the end of suffering, and that of the path to that end, named from both the aspect of the object, and from the sphere of their activity; (9) the knowledge of the end, insofar as we have accomplished all that we need to; and (10) the knowledge that nothing undesirable will ever grow again, named from our understanding of how causes bring things to multiply.

rows.english: In response, we might point out that—since you are here referring to something as the “family quality” insofar as, when one focuses upon it, that becomes a cause for the qualities of a realized being—then we would have to say that this is no great thing. rows.english: Now as a general note, the meaning of the Tibetan word sang-ngak, or way of the secret word, is "that which is performed or attained by acting in secret."  This is especially true for the more secret practices such as the secret world of the body. Speaking of these things to other people is the ultimate cause for the degeneration of your own attainments.  Insofar as I have set down a description of the secret world of the body in this recitation text, you should not show it to just anyone; but rather you should keep it under tight lock and key.  This point is extremely important.

rows.english: Here, moreover, is what they mean by the expression "end of all mysteries."  The root tantra of Highest Bliss includes those lines that go, Insofar as there are These absolute divisions into The open, action, activity, Deep practice and the end Of all the mysteries. Now the word "open" here refers to the open teachings, the way of the perfections.  "Action" is a reference to the Action Group of the secret teachings; "activity" to the Activity Group; and "deep practice" to the Group of Deep Practice.  The "end of all the mysteries" is an allusion then to the ultimate teachings of the way of the secret word: those of the Unsurpassed Group.  The word "division" here is a brief way of saying "one of the traditional groups among the secret teachings."

rows.acip: RO MA'I KHA STENG DANG RKYANG MA'I KHA 'OG TU PHYOGS PAR BSHAD PA'I RGYU MTSAN YOD DE, RO MAS MGRIN PA'I PHYOGS NAS SKYES PA LA STENG DU KHRAG 'PHEN 'DZIN GYI BYA BA BYED CING , RKYANG MAS LTE BA'I PHYOGS NAS 'OG TU KHU BA 'PHEN 'DZIN GYI BYA BA BYED PAS DE LTAR BSHAD PA YIN GYI, SPYIR DE GNYIS KYI STENG 'OG GI BUG PA NAS RLUNG 'BYUNG 'JUG BYED BA LA KHYAD PAR MED PA'I PHYIR,
rows.wylie: ro ma'i kha steng dang rkyang ma'i kha 'og tu phyogs par bshad pa'i rgyu mtshan yod de, ro mas mgrin pa'i phyogs nas skyes pa la steng du khrag 'phen 'dzin gyi bya ba byed cing , rkyang mas lte ba'i phyogs nas 'og tu khu ba 'phen 'dzin gyi bya ba byed pas de ltar bshad pa yin gyi, spyir de gnyis kyi steng 'og gi bug pa nas rlung 'byung 'jug byed ba la khyad par med pa'i phyir
rows.english: Now there is a reason why they say that the channel of taste faces upwards, while the solitary channel faces downwards.  In a male, the channel of taste performs the function of releasing and retaining the flow of the blood element from the throat on up.  The solitary channel then performs the same function for the flow of the semen element, from the navel on down. And although this is the case, there is in general no difference between these two channels insofar as the how the inner wind is made to exit and enter through their upper and lower openings.

rows.wylie: rgyu tshul gyi khyad par yod de, srog 'dzin, thur sel, mnyam gnas, gyen rgyu, khyab byed rnams rim pa bzhin du sna bug gnyis gnas dal bar rgyu ba dang, gnyis ka nas drag tu rgyu ba dang, g-yon rkyang nas dal bar rgyu ba dang, g-yas rkyang nas drag tu rgyu ba dang, gzhi la 'chi dus ma gtogs mi rgyu ba'i phyir
rows.english: There is furthermore a distinction between these winds insofar as the way in which they flow. Here is a list for the primary winds: 1) Life-holding wind: flows gently through both nostrils 2) Downward-clearing wind: flows roughly through both nostrils 3) Equal wind: flows gently, but only through the left nostril 4)  Upward-running wind: flows roughly, only through the right nostril 5) Pervasive wind: in the normal condition of things, doesn't flow at all, except during the death process.
